narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three pieces of information drove that decision, ranked by importance. First, your third-year class ranking was very low—you placed in the bottom decile of your school. This was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Second, your LSAT score of 40 was actually higher than the average of students who were accepted (37.2). This worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward passing, but not enough to overcome the other signals. Third, your first-year class ranking was also in the bottom decile, compared with an average around 6 for accepted students. This further increased the predicted risk of failing the bar.

Your low undergraduate GPA of 2.2 (versus 3.23 for accepted students) and low family income added some additional concern, though they were not the main drivers.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and class standing if you retake courses or pursue a post-baccalaureate program. Raising your LSAT further could also help offset weaker areas. Consider reapplying once you have clearer evidence that you can perform at the level needed to pass the bar on the first try.
